question: What is the main goal of selective toxicity when using antimicrobial drugs?

options.A: Preventing the drug from dissolving too quickly
options.B: Boosting the patient's natural immune system response
options.C: Broadening the range of bacteria the drug kills
options.D: Destroying the pathogen without harming host cells

explanation: Selective toxicity means the medication targets and kills the invading germ while keeping the mother's or baby's own cells safe from harm. [learn more](BMP124_U4_T1#BMP124_U4_T1_h1)

question: When should a midwife expect to use empiric antimicrobial therapy?

options.A: Only after all laboratory test results are fully confirmed
options.B: At the very end of a failed course of narrow-spectrum treatment
options.C: When the patient shows an allergy to standard first-line drugs
options.D: Before laboratory culture and sensitivity results are ready

explanation: Empiric treatment starts right away based on clinical signs and common local germs while waiting for lab tests to confirm the exact cause. [learn more](BMP124_U4_T1#BMP124_U4_T1_h1)

question: How do beta-lactamase enzymes protect bacteria from certain drugs?

options.A: By pumping the drug out through special cell wall channels
options.B: By thickening the outer capsule to block drug entry completely
options.C: By breaking down the chemical structure of the medication
options.D: By changing the shape of the internal bacterial ribosomes

explanation: Bacteria that produce beta-lactamase release enzymes that cut the chemical ring of susceptible drugs, making the medication useless against the infection. [learn more](BMP124_U4_T1#BMP124_U4_T1_h2)

question: What happens when bacteria develop active efflux pumps?

options.A: The drug is expelled from the bacterial cell before it can work
options.B: The drug binds permanently to harmless proteins in the bloodstream
options.C: The bacterial cell wall becomes completely impenetrable to water
options.D: The pathogen starts producing its own natural antimicrobial agents

explanation: Efflux pumps act like tiny revolving doors that push entering antimicrobial drugs straight back out before they can cause any damage. [learn more](BMP124_U4_T1#BMP124_U4_T1_h2)

question: Which of the following does NOT drive antimicrobial resistance in the community?

options.A: Purchasing leftover drugs without a professional prescription
options.B: Sharing remaining medications among family members
options.C: Completing the full prescribed dosage of antibiotics
options.D: Using broad-spectrum agents for simple viral infections

explanation: Finishing a prescribed drug course clears the infection completely. Stopping early or misusing drugs is what actually drives resistance. [learn more](BMP124_U4_T1#BMP124_U4_T1_h3)

question: A patient wants to buy strong antibiotics over the counter for a mild cold. What is the main danger of this practice?

options.A: Causing an immediate allergic reaction in the liver tissue
options.B: Promoting drug-resistant strains of bacteria in the community
options.C: Lowering the patient's normal body temperature too quickly
options.D: Killing all beneficial fungi in the upper respiratory tract

explanation: Using antibiotics when they are not needed exposes normal bacteria to the drug, allowing resistant strains to survive, multiply, and spread. [learn more](BMP124_U4_T1#BMP124_U4_T1_h3)

question: What is the main purpose of antimicrobial stewardship programs in healthcare?

options.A: Replacing all injectable medications with oral syrups and tablets
options.B: Promoting the safe, appropriate, and effective use of anti-infective drugs
options.C: Reducing the financial cost of hospital building maintenance and cleaning
options.D: Ensuring that every patient admitted to the ward receives prophylactic drugs

explanation: Stewardship helps ensure drugs are used correctly to get the best clinical results while preventing side effects and slowing down drug resistance. [learn more](BMP124_U4_T1#BMP124_U4_T1_h4)

question: How do basic infection control measures like hand hygiene support antimicrobial stewardship?

options.A: By preventing infections from spreading, reducing the need for drug therapy
options.B: By directly neutralizing resistant bacterial enzymes on the skin surface
options.C: By shortening the time required for laboratory culture results
options.D: By increasing the absorption rate of oral antibiotics in the gut

explanation: Stopping the spread of germs means fewer people get sick in the first place, which naturally cuts down the total number of antibiotics needed. [learn more](BMP124_U4_T1#BMP124_U4_T1_h4)

question: Why is it incorrect to use leftover antibiotics for a new illness later?

options.A: Leftover pills always change color and become toxic to the kidneys
options.B: The leftover drug may be the wrong type and might have lost potency
options.C: Antibiotics always expire within forty-eight hours of opening the bottle
options.D: Using old drugs automatically triggers an immediate anaphylactic shock

explanation: Different illnesses need specific medications. Also, older medications often break down over time and fail to kill bacteria effectively. [learn more](BMP124_U4_T1#BMP124_U4_T1_h5)

question: A postpartum mother says she stopped her prescribed antibiotics after three days because her wound stopped hurting. What is your best response?

options.A: Tell her to double the dose tomorrow to make up for the missed days
options.B: Praise her for saving money and suggest keeping the rest for her baby
options.C: Explain that stopping early leaves strong germs alive and advise completing the dose
options.D: Agree that pain is the only indicator of active bacterial infection

explanation: Midwives teach mothers that feeling better does not mean the infection is fully gone. Stopping early allows stronger bacteria to survive and cause drug resistance. [learn more](BMP124_U4_T1#BMP124_U4_T1_h5)
